title: Decoupling Universal Laws and Environmental Heterogeneity
one_liner: Split spatio-temporal dynamics into a universal diffusion law and environment-specific patterns, using physics equations to predict accurately when conditions change.
lead: Most forecasting models learn one pattern from their training data, but the real world keeps changing. When a city's traffic patterns shift or weather deviates, the model breaks. This paper splits the problem into two pieces: the universal physics (how things naturally spread and change) and the local environment (the specific makeup of each place). By using physics equations instead of black-box neural guesses, it stays accurate even when dropped into new cities or changed conditions.

problem.h2: Why today's forecasting breaks when conditions shift
paras: A forecasting model trained on one year of a city's traffic learns a pattern: rush hour congestion, weekend quiet, seasonal rhythms. But it learned that ONE city's specific pattern. If you move the model to a different city, it flops. Or if conditions change—a new highway opens, a pandemic hits, a heat wave arrives—the model's learned pattern no longer matches reality.

Existing fix: throw in graph neural networks that update their connections based on the data. But this is brittle. It treats every local difference as a separate discrete object to learn, like having to memorize a thousand different traffic rules instead of understanding the underlying physics. The universal laws (things spread and flow according to physics) get tangled up with the local quirks (this city is hilly, that one is flat). You cannot disentangle them, so when you move to a new place or conditions shift, the model has no portable foundation.

callout.b: The paper's move, in one sentence:
callout.html: Use physics equations to separate the universal spreading mechanism from environment-specific local properties, so the core law travels to new places but adapts to local conditions.

steps.text: Rewrite forecasting as an inhomogeneous PDE (partial differential equation)—the math that describes how things evolve in space and time.
Extract an Invariant Diffusion Operator (how things spread everywhere) and an Environment Basis Manifold (the local properties of each place).

steps.b: Approximate the spreading with a weighted sum
steps.text: The Green's function of the Laplacian (the universal spread pattern) is approximated by a weighted sum mechanism (how much each other point influences this one), keeping computation fast.

steps.b: Add random environment shifts during training
steps.text: Randomly shift the local environment properties during training so the model learns to handle environmental changes, because seeing varied environments forces the universal law to work across all of them, not just memorize one city's exact setup.

steps.b: Test on new cities and shifted conditions
steps.text: Verify the universal law transfers while local coefficients adapt to new environments.

object.h2: The one thing the paper changes
paras: Instead of a monolithic neural network that bakes both universal and local patterns together, the paper splits the learned model into two disentangled pieces: the invariant spreading mechanism (the Diffusion Operator) and the flexible local environment encoding (a smooth surface in mathematical space that represents all the possible local environments). This separation lets each piece be controlled independently.
object.object: Model decomposition into universal law and environment encoding

hidden.h2: The hidden quantity: Importance of each environment property
hidden.name: Environment Basis coefficients
paras: The paper measures how much each local environmental property (terrain elevation, building density, water bodies, etc.) matters for accurate predictions. These coefficients tell you which environmental features drive heterogeneity in each place.

The paper estimates these by storing a low-dimensional manifold (a smooth surface in mathematical space) that captures environment-specific variation. During training, it learns which directions on this manifold correspond to real physical differences that matter for forecasting. When you move to a new city, you solve for new basis coefficients without retraining the universal law.

heat.caption: Darker means that environment property has stronger influence on local forecasts.

reads.html: Some environmental features (like terrain roughness) have huge impact on how wind and water spread. Others barely matter. The hidden quantity is this impact score for each environmental feature.
The basis coefficients on the environment manifold encode the relative importance of each learned direction in environment space. They control the non-uniform (environment-specific) term in the PDE.

mechanism.h2: Why decoupling the law from the environment works
paras: Physics tells us that spreading (diffusion) obeys the same rules everywhere—heat spreads via the same law whether in a desert or a forest. But the medium is different: sand conducts heat differently than soil. The paper exploits this insight. It factorizes the model into a universal operator (how things spread, period) and a local manifold (what the medium is like here).

The universal law is encoded as an Invariant Diffusion Operator, which uses linear attention to approximate the Laplacian Green's function—the mathematical description of how a disturbance at one point influences all others via diffusion. This operator works anywhere because it captures the physics, not the specifics of one place.

The local environment is encoded as a low-dimensional manifold of basis directions (each direction represents a blend of environmental properties). Each city is represented by a set of coefficients on this manifold. When you move to a new city, the universal law stays fixed, but you solve for new environmental coefficients using just a few data points. This is few-shot transfer: you reuse the physics engine but reprogram the local conditions.

During training, random shifts perturb the environment coefficients. This forces the universal law to learn to work across a range of conditions, not just overfit to one city's exact properties. The result is a model that handles distribution shift (when real conditions differ from training data) because it has seen and adapted to environmental changes.

stages.s: Extract local environment coefficients from the data
Apply universal Diffusion Operator (spreading via Green's function)

math.h2: The math: inhomogeneous PDE with factorized dynamics
math.words: The evolution of the field is governed by: a universal diffusion operator multiplied by spatially-varying diffusion coefficients that depend on the local environment. In integral form, the value at a point is the sum over all other points of (the Green's function times the field value there, weighted by local properties).
math.equation: u_t(x, t) = L_inv[u] + c(x) * nabla^2 u(x, t)
symbols: field value at position x and time t (e.g. traffic density, temperature)
invariant diffusion operator (the universal law, independent of environment)
spatially-varying diffusion coefficient (depends on local environment properties)
Laplacian (measures how different a point is from its neighbors)

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Example: a city grid 3x3. Center cell has traffic density 10, all neighbors have 8.
Laplacian at center: (8+8+8+8+8+8-6*10) / cell_area = -6 (denser than surroundings, will spread out).
Without environment scaling (c=1): density change = -6 per time step.
City A has c=0.5 (slow spread, congested streets): density change = 0.5 * (-6) = -3 per step.
City B has c=1.5 (fast spread, open roads): density change = 1.5 * (-6) = -9 per step.
Same universal law (Laplacian), but each city's local property (c) sets the spreading speed.

math.note: The Invariant Diffusion Operator is the Laplacian; the Environment Basis Manifold controls the local scaling coefficients c(x).

bars.h2: How much better does splitting help?

charts.title: Old approach: single neural model
charts.note: Model has memorized one city's patterns. It has no portable knowledge to transfer.

charts.title: This paper: split law and environment
charts.note: Universal law transfers everywhere. Environment adaptation is fast and reliable.

items.html: If the manifold does not have enough dimensions, it cannot capture the real environmental variation. New cities may not fit well on the learned manifold, and transfer fails.
If you randomize the environment during training too much, the model learns to ignore local properties and falls back to generic diffusion, losing accuracy within-city.

If the true dynamics are not actually diffusion-like (e.g. if there is discontinuous turbulence or phase transitions), the PDE form will not capture them, no matter how smart the environment encoding is.

When the basis is large enough, perturbations are tuned carefully, and the problem is genuinely diffusion-dominated, transfer to new cities works in few-shot mode and forecasting on data from different distributions stays accurate.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a small spatio-temporal dataset (e.g. simulated heat diffusion on a grid, or synthetic traffic on a toy city network). Train STPDE on City A for 50 time steps. Then freeze the Invariant Diffusion Operator and solve for the environment basis coefficients of City B using only 5 data points from City B. Compare the few-shot transfer accuracy against a baseline model fine-tuned normally on City B. Also add a distribution shift (change a global setting like ambient temperature) partway through and verify STPDE handles it better than the baseline, because the universal law was trained to work across many environment shifts so it adapts naturally, while the baseline was trained on only one temperature regime.
demo.metric_eq: Transfer accuracy = (forecast error on City B with frozen law) / (forecast error without transfer prior); should be > 1.5 (i.e. at least 50% better than random initialization).
demo.closing: The demo must make clear that the universal law learned from City A works immediately on City B, asking only for a few environment coefficients, while a naive model would fail on City B until fully retrained.
